keyVerseText: Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred shekels, and of sweet cinnamon half so much, even two hundred and fifty shekels, and of sweet calamus two hundred and fifty shekels,
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun דְּרוֹר (dᵉrôwr) originates from an unused root meaning 'to move rapidly,' which conveys a sense of flowing or free movement. This etymology enriches the common English gloss of 'liberty' by emphasizing not only freedom but also an unrestrained, spontaneous outflow, suggesting purity and clarity. Thus, the root sense highlights both physical and metaphorical freedom as a dynamic, life-giving flow rather than mere absence of restraint.
usageInScripture: The word דְּרוֹר appears eight times in the Hebrew Bible and is predominantly translated as 'liberty' or 'a liberty,' showing a consistent theme of freedom. It is notably used in contexts such as the proclamation of liberty during the Jubilee year and in reference to pure myrrh, indicating both tangible and symbolic expressions of freedom and purity. This range from physical substances to social and spiritual release reveals the word’s versatile yet focused meaning centered on unbounded movement and release.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding דְּרוֹר as more than mere freedom but as a flowing, pure liberty enriches our grasp of biblical freedom as something active and life-giving, rooted in God’s design. In Scripture, liberty is not just a legal status but a divine provision that restores and refreshes, as seen in the Jubilee year’s release of debts and slaves. This dynamic freedom points forward to the ultimate liberty found in Christ, who sets believers free from sin’s bondage, enabling a pure and spontaneous outflow of new life. Thus, דְּרוֹר underscores the gospel’s promise of liberation that is both inward and outward, spiritual and practical.
keyVerseReflection: Exodus 30:23 mentions 'pure myrrh' using the word דְּרוֹר to describe its flowing, fine quality. Here, the term highlights the essence of purity and free movement, which enriches the understanding of the sacred anointing oil’s ingredients. This use of דְּרוֹר connects the physical purity of the myrrh with the spiritual liberty God grants, suggesting that the holiness of worship involves both purity and freedom flowing from God’s presence.
